mainTopic: רב הונא's oath for a lost משכון, the jewels case of רב נחמן, and the rule that property taken by שומא can be bought back.
overview: The amud opens with a problem. רב הונא says the creditor holding a משכון must swear it is no longer with him. But the משנה worries that the creditor might later produce the item. רבא, רב יוסף, אביי and רב אשי each answer in turn. In the end, רב אשי says both sides swear and the משנה only tells us that the מלוה swears first. Next, רבא refutes רב הונא from a later clause of the משנה. רב כהנא answers that the case is one where the borrower trusts the lender. The גמרא then explains, with a פסוק from משלי, why that trust runs only one way. Then comes the story of jewels a שומר could not find. רב נחמן made him pay with his house, but when the jewels turned up, everything went back to its owner. This leads to the rule that land taken by שומא can always be bought back by the debtor, because of 'וְעָשִׂיתָ הַיָּשָׁר וְהַטּוֹב'. The amud closes by showing who must give such land back and who need not, including a husband, who counts as a buyer according to the תקנת אושא.

steps.title: If the creditor already swore, how can he produce the collateral?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה's reason using רב הונא's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: If רב הונא is right that the creditor swears the collateral is not in his possession, how could he later bring it out?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא puts רב הונא's rule next to the משנה and finds a problem. The משנה worries the creditor will produce the collateral, but he already swore he doesn't have it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gives the oath to the מלוה instead of the לוה, because otherwise the לוה might swear and then the creditor might produce the משכון. According to רב הונא, the creditor must swear it is not in his possession. Once he has sworn that, the fear that he will produce it seems to disappear.

keyTerms.meaning: If רב הונא's statement is correct
The lender or creditor, who is holding the collateral
That it is not in his possession

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not against רב הונא himself. It asks how the משנה's reason can still make sense if רב הונא is right.

phrases.english: If the statement of Rav Huna is so,
since the creditor swears
that it is not in his possession,
how can he produce it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתָא לִדְרַב הוּנָא כֵּיוָן דְּמִשְׁתְּבַע מִלְוֶה
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's reason ("lest the creditor produce the collateral") when combined with רב הונא's oath
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The creditor already swore it is not with him, so he cannot later produce it. The משנה's worry becomes pointless.

steps.title: רבא: the case is where witnesses saw it burn
steps.stepSummary: רבא sets the משנה in a case where witnesses saw the collateral burn, so no possession oath is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: the משנה is talking about where there are witnesses that it was burned.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers that the משנה's case has witnesses to the loss. Then the creditor does not need רב הונא's oath at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא's oath is only needed when we can't verify the loss. If witnesses saw the collateral burn, the creditor doesn't swear that it isn't with him. So the conflict seems to go away.

phrases.english: Rava said:
where there are witnesses that it was burned.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 1 by narrowing the case
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the משנה to a specific case (אוקימתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה's case requires the creditor's possession oath.
steps.terutzMaskana: Witnesses saw it burn, so no possession oath is needed.

steps.title: If it burned, how could he ever bring it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רבא: burned collateral can never be produced, so the משנה's worry makes no sense.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, from where would he bring it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבא. If the collateral burned, it is gone forever, so there is no fear that the creditor will produce it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's case removes רב הונא's oath, but it also removes the משנה's reason. The משנה worries the creditor might bring out the item. Ashes can't be brought out.

keyTerms.meaning: From where would he bring it?

phrases.english: If so,
from where would he bring it?

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Burned collateral can never be produced, so the משנה's reason doesn't fit.

steps.title: רב יוסף: the case is where witnesses saw it stolen
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף sets the משנה in a case of theft with witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב יוסף said: where there are witnesses that it was stolen.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף replaces רבא's answer. The case is that witnesses saw the collateral get stolen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Theft with witnesses still removes the need for the possession oath, because the loss is proven. Unlike burning, a stolen item still exists somewhere.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Yosef said:
where there are witnesses that it was stolen.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: שֶׁיֵּשׁ עֵדִים שֶׁנִּגְנְבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רבא's rejected answer
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The case is burning, where nothing can be produced.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is theft, where the item still exists.

steps.title: Even if stolen, how would he bring it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks that stolen collateral is also out of the creditor's hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: Ultimately, from where would he bring it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב יוסף. A stolen item is with the thief, so how would the creditor produce it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same question as before comes back in a weaker form. Theft still leaves the creditor without the item, so the משנה's fear still seems unlikely.

phrases.english: Ultimately, from where would he bring it?

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A stolen item is also out of reach, so the fear of producing it remains unclear.

steps.title: He might track down the thief and bring it
steps.stepSummary: The creditor might work hard, find the thief, and bring the collateral back.
steps.simpleTranslation: He might exert himself and bring it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the creditor could put in effort, find the thief, and recover the collateral.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike burning, theft leaves a real chance of getting the item back. If that happened after the לוה swore, the לוה's oath about its value could be shown false. That is why the oath is given to the מלוה instead.

phrases.english: That he exerts himself and brings it.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that the case is realistic
steps.terutzMaskana: The creditor may recover it from the thief.

steps.title: Then the borrower could also find it
steps.stepSummary: If the creditor can track it down, so can the borrower. So why is one order better than the other?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, when the creditor swears too, let the borrower exert himself and bring it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks: if recovery is possible, the borrower could also recover it after the creditor swears. Then neither order protects anyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה moves the oath from the לוה to the מלוה so that the לוה's oath won't be shown false. But the מלוה's oath could equally be shown false if the לוה found the item. So why favor one side?

phrases.aramaic: אִי הָכִי, כִּי מִשְׁתְּבַע מַלְוֶה נָמֵי,
phrases.english: If so, when the creditor swears too,
let the borrower exert himself and bring it!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, כִּי מִשְׁתְּבַע מַלְוֶה נָמֵי, לִטְרַח לֹוֶה וְלַיְתֵי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same risk applies to the creditor's oath, so the order of oaths seems not to matter.

steps.title: Only the creditor knows who visits his house
steps.stepSummary: The creditor can guess who the thief is because he knows who visits his house. The borrower cannot.
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, the creditor knows who comes in and out of his house, and he goes and works to bring it. But does the borrower know who comes in and out of the creditor's house?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two sides are not equal. The creditor has leads on the thief, and the borrower has none.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The theft happened in the creditor's home, so he knows who might have taken it. Recovery by the creditor is realistic, but recovery by the borrower is not. So the risk is only to the לוה's oath, and the oath is given to the מלוה.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רב יוסף, the משנה deals with witnessed theft. The oath goes to the creditor instead of the borrower because only the creditor can realistically track down the thief.

phrases.english: Granted, the creditor knows
who comes in and goes out of his house,
and he goes and exerts himself and brings it.
But the borrower, does he know
who comes in and goes out of the creditor's house?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא מַלְוֶה יָדַע מַאן קָא עָיֵיל וְנָפֵק בְּבֵיתֵיהּ
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the two cases are different
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sides are equally able to recover the item.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the creditor has realistic leads on the thief.

steps.title: אביי: a decree in case he claims he found it after the oath
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains the משנה as a rabbinic decree. The creditor might produce the item and claim he found it only after the oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי says: it is a decree, in case he claims and tells him, "I found it after the oath."
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a different answer to the original question in step 1. Even after swearing, the creditor could bring out the collateral and say he found it later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא's oath does not stop the creditor from producing the item later. He can claim his oath was true when he made it and the item turned up afterward. To avoid that situation after the לוה swears, the חכמים made a גזירה that the oath goes to the מלוה instead of the לוה. This works without needing a special case of witnesses.

phrases.english: Abaye says: it is a decree
lest he claim and say to him:
phrases.notes: The one making the claim is the creditor, speaking to the borrower.

phrases.english: I found it after the oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new answer to step 1, separate from רבא and רב יוסף
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining the rule as a protective decree
steps.terutzHavaAmina: After swearing, the creditor can never produce the item.
steps.terutzMaskana: He could produce it and claim he found it after the oath, so the חכמים decreed that the oath goes to him instead of the borrower.

steps.title: רב אשי: both sides swear
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the creditor swears it is not with him, and the borrower swears how much it was worth.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: this one swears and that one swears. This one swears that it is not in his possession, and that one swears how much it was worth.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a third answer. Both oaths happen: the creditor's oath from רב הונא, and the borrower's oath about the value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי does not drop either oath. The creditor swears it is not with him, and the borrower swears about its value. This sets up his reading of the משנה in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: This one swears and that one swears

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
This one swears and that one swears,
this one swears that it is not in his possession,
and that one swears how much it was worth.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: זֶה נִשְׁבָּע וְזֶה נִשְׁבָּע
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה's oath replaces the borrower's oath.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both swear, each about something different.

steps.title: The משנה only tells us who swears first
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי reads the משנה as setting the order: the creditor swears first, so the borrower won't swear and then the creditor produce the item.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what it means: who swears first? The creditor swears first, lest this one swear and the other produce the deposit.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי rereads the משנה's question "who swears?" as "who swears first?", and the answer is the מלוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the creditor has sworn it is not with him, he is committed to that position. Then the borrower can safely swear about its value. If the borrower swore first, the creditor might bring out the item and show the borrower's oath was false.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what it means

steps.whatToRemember: There are three ways to fit רב הונא with the משנה. רב יוסף: a case of witnessed theft. אביי: a גזירה in case of "I found it later." רב אשי: both swear, and the משנה only sets the order.
steps.whyThisMatters: According to רב אשי, רב הונא's oath and the משנה's oath can both stand together. The משנה is only about the order of the oaths.

phrases.english: And this is what it is saying: who swears first?
The creditor swears first,
lest this one swear
and the other produce the deposit.
phrases.notes: "The other" is the creditor, and "the deposit" is the collateral he was holding.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב אשי's answer by rereading the משנה
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The משנה is about the order of the oaths. The creditor swears first that it is not with him, and then the borrower swears about its value.

steps.title: רבא's refutation of רב הונא from the משנה
steps.stepSummary: רבא argues that the משנה, which exempts the מלוה when they argue over the משכון's value, contradicts רב הונא's rule that the מלוה must swear the משכון is not with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בר תחליפא said in the name of רבא: the first part of the later clause of the משנה refutes רב הונא. The borrower says, 'You lent me a סלע on it, and it was worth two.' The lender says, 'No, I lent you a סלע on it, and it was worth one סלע.' The lender is exempt. But if רב הונא is right, then since the lender already has to swear that the item is not in his possession, he should also have to swear, through גלגול שבועה, how much it was worth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a challenge against רב הונא from a case in the משנה where the lender walks away with no oath at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא said that a lender who claims the משכון was lost must swear it is not with him. If he must take that oath anyway, the rule of גלגול שבועה lets the court add an oath about the item's value. Yet the משנה says the lender is completely exempt, which suggests no oath was required in the first place.

keyTerms.meaning: The first part of the later clause of the משנה
Since, or because (here: since he already has to swear)
Rolling extra claims into an oath someone already has to take

steps.confusionAlert: Here the borrower is the one making the claim. He says the משכון was worth more than the loan, so the lender owes him the difference.

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא בַּר תַּחְלִיפָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא אָמַר:
phrases.english: Rav Huna bar Taḥlifa said in the name of Rava:
The first part of the latter clause is a refutation of Rav Huna,
phrases.notes: This is the רב הונא from earlier, who required the lender's oath, not the speaker, רב הונא בר תחליפא.

phrases.aramaic: סֶלַע הִלְוִיתַנִי עָלָיו, שְׁתַּיִם הָיָה שָׁוֶה.
phrases.english: 'You lent me a sela on it, it was worth two.'
And the other says: 'Not so,'
'rather, I lent you a sela on it,'
'it was worth a sela.' He is exempt.
And if Rav Huna's view is correct,
since the lender swears that it is not in his possession,
let him also swear, by extension of the oath,
how much it was worth!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge against רב הונא's oath requirement, based on the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's rule that the מלוה swears the משכון is not in his possession
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An oath he must already take would carry a rolled-in oath about value through גלגול שבועה, yet the משנה exempts him completely.

steps.title: רב כהנא: the borrower trusts the lender
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא answers that the משנה is speaking where the לוה believes the מלוה that the משכון is lost, so no oath is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: I said this teaching in front of רב כהנא, and he told me: the משנה is talking about a case where the borrower trusts the lender.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי reports an answer he heard from רב כהנא that saves רב הונא's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the borrower himself believes the lender that the item is gone, there is no oath to take that it is not with him. With no main oath, there is nothing to attach a rolled-in oath about value to, so the lender is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it be a case where he trusts him

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
I said this teaching before Rav Kahana,
and he said to me: Let it be where he trusts him.
phrases.notes: The borrower trusts the lender that the משכון really is lost.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the refutation in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה shows that a lender never swears the משכון is not with him.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is a special case where the borrower trusts the lender, so no oath is required.

steps.title: Then trust him about the value too
steps.stepSummary: If the לוה trusts the מלוה, why not trust him about how much the משכון was worth as well?
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let the borrower also trust the lender on this point, how much it was worth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב כהנא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the borrower believes the lender about the loss, there should be no argument over value either. The משנה, though, describes the two of them arguing about value.

phrases.english: But let the borrower also trust the lender
in this, how much it was worth?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב כהנא's answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the borrower trusts the lender
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone who trusts the lender should trust him all the way, including about the value.

steps.title: The lender doesn't really know its value
steps.stepSummary: The לוה trusts the מלוה's honesty but not his knowledge, because the item was never the lender's.
steps.simpleTranslation: The lender does not know its value for certain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the borrower's trust stops at the question of value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Trusting someone not to lie is different from trusting him to know the facts. The lender might honestly be wrong about the value of someone else's object.

phrases.english: He is not certain about it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 14.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Trust about the loss should mean trust about the value too.
steps.terutzMaskana: The borrower trusts the lender's honesty but not his knowledge of the value.

steps.title: Then let the lender trust the borrower
steps.stepSummary: The לוה knows his own item's value, so why doesn't the מלוה simply believe him?
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let the lender trust the borrower, since the borrower knows its value for certain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the argument doesn't end from the other side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower owns the item, so he surely knows what it was worth. If the lender believed him, there would be no argument at all.

phrases.english: But let the lender trust the borrower,
since he is certain about it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A follow-up challenge built on the answer in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: Why the argument over value exists at all
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The borrower has the knowledge, so the lender should rely on him.

steps.title: The lender doesn't trust the borrower
steps.stepSummary: The מלוה does not trust the לוה's honesty.
steps.simpleTranslation: The lender does not trust him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the lender simply doesn't believe the borrower.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So the trust runs only one way. The borrower trusts the lender's honesty, but the lender does not trust the borrower's honesty.

phrases.english: He does not trust him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Trust that runs only one way
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The lender should accept the borrower's figure.
steps.terutzMaskana: The lender doesn't trust the borrower's honesty.

steps.title: Why does the trust go only one way?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the לוה trusts the מלוה, but the מלוה does not trust the לוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about the borrower, that he trusts the lender? And what is different about the lender, that he does not trust the borrower?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the one-way trust described in the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 13 through 17 assumed the borrower trusts the lender while the lender doesn't trust the borrower. Now the גמרא wants to know why that makes sense.

phrases.aramaic: וּמַאי שְׁנָא לֹוֶה דִּמְהֵימַן לֵיהּ לְמַלְוֶה,
phrases.english: And what is different about the borrower, that he trusts the lender,

phrases.aramaic: וּמַאי שְׁנָא מַלְוֶה דְּלָא מְהֵימַן לֵיהּ לְלֹוֶה?
phrases.english: and what is different about the lender, that he does not trust the borrower?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאי שְׁנָא לֹוֶה דִּמְהֵימַן לֵיהּ לְמַלְוֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind steps 13 and 17.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the trust runs only from borrower to lender

steps.title: How each one views the other, from משלי
steps.stepSummary: The לוה sees the מלוה as upright and rewarded with wealth. The מלוה sees the לוה as crooked and punished with poverty.
steps.simpleTranslation: The borrower applies to the lender the verse 'The integrity of the upright guides them.' The lender applies to the borrower the verse 'And the crookedness of the treacherous destroys them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers using two halves of one פסוק, showing how each side thinks about the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower assumes the lender has money because he is honest and blessed for it. The lender assumes the borrower is poor because he is dishonest. These attitudes explain why the trust runs only one way.

keyTerms.meaning: Applies to him, sees fulfilled in him

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה exempts the lender only where the borrower trusts him about the loss. Even then, the borrower doesn't rely on the lender's knowledge of the value, and the lender doesn't trust the borrower's honesty.

phrases.english: The borrower applies to the lender
'The integrity of the upright shall guide them,'
the lender applies to the borrower
'But the perverseness of the faithless shall destroy them.'
phrases.notes: This is the second half of the same פסוק.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Each side views the other through a פסוק: the lender as upright, the borrower as crooked.

steps.title: The story of the deposited jewels
steps.stepSummary: A שומר who was given jewels claims he doesn't know where he put them, and the case comes to רב נחמן.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man deposited jewels with his friend. He said to him, 'Give me my jewels.' The friend said, 'I don't know where I put them.' The owner came before רב נחמן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story about a פקדון. This step sets up the case for רב נחמן's ruling in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The שומר doesn't claim the jewels were stolen or lost by accident. He says he simply doesn't know where they are, and that kind of claim needs a ruling.

phrases.aramaic: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דְּאַפְקֵיד כִּיפֵּי גַּבֵּי חַבְרֵיהּ.
phrases.english: A certain man deposited jewels with his friend.
He said to him: Give me my jewels.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לָא יָדַעְנָא הֵיכָא אוֹתְבִי[תִי]נְהוּ.
phrases.english: He said to him: I don't know where I put them.
phrases.notes: The letters in square brackets are the corrected spelling of the word 'I put them.'

phrases.english: He came before Rav Naḥman.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דְּאַפְקֵיד כִּיפֵּי גַּבֵּי חַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story, separate from the משכון discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case of a שומר who says he doesn't know where he put the deposit.

steps.title: רב נחמן: 'I don't know' is negligence
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן rules that saying 'I don't know' counts as פשיעה. When the שומר refuses to pay, רב נחמן has his house taken from him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to him: any 'I don't know' is negligence, so go pay. He didn't pay. רב נחמן went and took his palace from him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן rules that the שומר must pay, then enforces the ruling by taking his house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שומר is supposed to keep track of what he was given. Not knowing where he put it is itself a failure to guard, so he pays as a negligent שומר.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a practical rule: a שומר who claims 'I don't know where I put it' is treated as negligent and must pay.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: כֹּל לָא יָדַעְנָא פְּשִׁיעוּתָא הִיא,
phrases.english: He said to him: Every 'I don't know' is negligence,
go pay! He did not pay.

phrases.aramaic: אֲזַל רַב נַחְמָן אַגַּבְּיֵהּ לְאַפַּדְנֵיהּ מִינֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: Rav Naḥman went and collected his palace from him,
phrases.notes: He had the שומר's house taken to pay the owner for the jewels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling on the case set up in step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Saying 'I don't know where I put it' is negligence, and the שומר must pay.

steps.title: The jewels are found and everything goes back
steps.stepSummary: The jewels turn up, now worth more. רב נחמן rules that the jewels go back to their owner and the house goes back to the שומר.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end the jewels were found, and they had gone up in value. רב נחמן said: the jewels go back to their owner, and the palace goes back to its owner.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with רב נחמן undoing the payment once the jewels are found.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking the house was only a payment for jewels that seemed to be gone. Once they are found, the payment is cancelled. The jewels, including their rise in value, belong to the original owner, and the שומר gets his house back without gaining from that increase.

keyTerms.meaning: They go back to their owners

steps.whatToRemember: A שומר who says 'I don't know where it is' must pay. But if the item is later found, the payment is undone, and the owner gets his item back along with any rise in its value.

phrases.english: In the end the jewels were found and had increased in value.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: הָדְרִי כִּיפֵּי לְמָרַיְיהוּ.
phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said: The jewels return to their owner.
And the palace returns to its owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the story and reverses the payment from step 21.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Once the item is found, the payment is undone: the owner gets back his jewels with their added value, and the שומר gets back his house.

steps.title: רבא's question: shouldn't the bailee keep the jewels?
steps.stepSummary: רבא recalls challenging רב נחמן with our משנה, where a שומר who pays rather than swear gets the item. רב נחמן did not answer him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: I was sitting in front of רב נחמן, and we were learning this chapter, 'One who deposits.' I said to him: This is like the case of the bailee who paid and did not want to swear, who then gets the item! And he did not answer me.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא tells how he challenged רב נחמן's ruling that the jewels go back to the owner. רב נחמן stayed silent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In our משנה, a שומר who pays instead of swearing gets ownership of the item, including any double payment from a thief. Here the שומר also paid, by losing his house. So רבא asks why he does not keep the jewels.

keyTerms.meaning: our chapter (the one we were learning)
he paid and did not want to swear (wording from our משנה)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָבָא: הֲוָה יָתֵיבְנָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן,
phrases.english: Rava said: I was sitting before Rav Nachman,
and our chapter was 'One who deposits,'

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲמַרִי לֵיהּ: שִׁילֵּם וְלֹא רָצָה לִישָּׁבַע.
phrases.english: and I said to him: 'He paid and did not want to swear!'
phrases.notes: He is quoting the משנה. That שומר paid instead of swearing, so the item becomes his.

phrases.english: And he did not answer me.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲמַרִי לֵיהּ: שִׁילֵּם וְלֹא רָצָה לִישָּׁבַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן's ruling in step 22 that the jewels go back to the owner.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's ruling that the jewels return to the owner
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Our משנה says a שומר who pays gets the item. This שומר paid, so the jewels should be his.

steps.title: The difference: this bailee dragged the owner to court
steps.stepSummary: רבא admits רב נחמן was right not to answer. A שומר who pays willingly is different from one who forces the owner to go to בית דין.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he did well not to answer me. Why? There, the bailee did not trouble the owner to go to court. Here, he troubled him to go to court.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers his own question. He explains why the משנה's case is different from the jewels case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the שומר paid on his own, so the owner gladly hands him ownership of the item. Here the שומר refused to pay and the owner had to go to בית דין. An owner treated like that does not give up his item to the שומר.

keyTerms.meaning: he troubled him, put him to effort

steps.whatToRemember: A שומר who pays willingly gets the item. A שומר who makes the owner fight in court does not.

phrases.english: And he did well that he did not answer me.
What is the reason?
There, he did not trouble him to go to court;
phrases.notes: 'There' is the משנה's case. 'He' is the שומר and 'him' is the owner.

phrases.english: here, he troubled him to go to court.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשַׁפִּיר עֲבַד דְּלָא אַהְדַּר לִי. מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 23 by showing the two cases are different.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any שומר who pays gets the deposit, as in the משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a שומר who pays willingly, without forcing the owner to court, gets the deposit.

steps.title: Does רב נחמן hold that a court appraisal can be reversed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether returning the house shows that רב נחמן holds property taken by שומא goes back once the debt is paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean that רב נחמן holds that property taken by appraisal goes back?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what we can learn from רב נחמן giving the house back to the שומר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The house was taken by the court through an appraisal (שומא) to pay the owner. Giving it back could mean that any שומא can be reversed. The גמרא checks whether that is really what רב נחמן holds.

keyTerms.meaning: is this to say? (testing what we can learn)
court appraisal; property taken to pay a debt at a value set by the court

phrases.english: Is this to say that Rav Nachman holds
that an appraisal goes back?
phrases.notes: He means: once the debtor pays, he gets back the property the court took from him.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמֵימְרָא דְּסָבַר רַב נַחְמָן דְּשׁוּמָא הָדַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a possible general rule from the house being returned in step 22.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רב נחמן holds that any שומא can be reversed.

steps.title: No: that appraisal was a mistake from the start
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the inference. The house went back only because the שומא was based on a mistake.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because the appraisal was a mistake, since the jewels were there from the beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the question. We cannot learn a general rule from the jewels case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The house was taken because everyone thought the jewels were lost. In fact the jewels were with the שומר the whole time. So the שומא was a mistake, and returning the house says nothing about a normal, correct שומא.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not say a שומא can never be reversed. It only says the jewels case cannot prove it, because that שומא was a mistake. The next steps deal with a normal שומא.

phrases.english: It is different there,
for the appraisal was a mistake,
since the jewels were there from the beginning.
phrases.notes: The printed גמרא has the word in round brackets. The corrected wording uses the word in square brackets. The meaning is the same.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference proposed in step 25.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects learning a general rule about שומא from the jewels case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The jewels case involved a mistaken שומא, so it is a special case.

steps.title: נהרדעא: an appraisal can be reversed for twelve months
steps.stepSummary: The חכמי נהרדעא rule that property taken by שומא goes back to the debtor if he pays within twelve months.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמי נהרדעא say: Property taken by appraisal goes back to the debtor, up to twelve months.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to a normal שומא and brings the view of the חכמי נהרדעא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A normal, correct שומא can still be undone. The debtor may pay the debt and take back his property, but only within twelve months.

phrases.english: The Sages of Neharde'a say:

phrases.aramaic: שׁוּמָא הָדַר עַד תְּרֵיסַר יַרְחֵי שַׁתָּא.
phrases.english: An appraisal goes back until twelve months of the year.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the jewels case to the general law of a normal שומא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A debtor can buy back property taken by שומא within twelve months.

steps.title: אמימר: an appraisal can always be reversed
steps.stepSummary: אמימר, though from נהרדעא himself, holds there is no time limit on reversing a שומא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And אמימר said: I myself am from נהרדעא, and I hold that an appraisal can always be reversed.
steps.whatsHappening: אמימר disagrees with the twelve-month limit of the חכמי נהרדעא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אמימר points out that he is from נהרדעא too, yet he does not accept their time limit. In his view, the debtor can pay and get his property back at any time.

phrases.english: And Ameimar said: I myself am from Neharde'a,
and I hold that an appraisal goes back forever.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the twelve-month limit in step 27.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שומא can be reversed at any time.

steps.title: The law: an appraisal can always be reversed, because it is right and good
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה follows אמימר, based on the פסוק 'וְעָשִׂיתָ הַיָּשָׁר וְהַטּוֹב'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is: an appraisal can always be reversed, because it says: 'And you shall do what is right and good.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rules like אמימר and gives the reason from a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the creditor has his money, it is 'right and good' to let the debtor have his own property back. So there is no time limit on reversing a שומא.

keyTerms.meaning: 'and you shall do what is right and good' (דברים 6:18)

steps.whatToRemember: The הלכה is that a debtor can always pay and take back property the court gave his creditor. The reason is 'וְעָשִׂיתָ הַיָּשָׁר וְהַטּוֹב'.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a practical rule in monetary law. It shows the תורה asks people to do what is fair and kind even beyond strict legal rights.

phrases.english: And the halacha is: an appraisal goes back forever,
because it says: 'And you shall do what is right and good.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the dispute between steps 27 and 28 in favor of אמימר.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A שומא can always be reversed when the debtor pays, because of 'וְעָשִׂיתָ הַיָּשָׁר וְהַטּוֹב'.

steps.title: A creditor's creditor must also give the land back
steps.stepSummary: If land was given by שומא to a בעל חוב and he passed it to his own בעל חוב by שומא, the original debtor can still pay and take it back. The second creditor is no better than the man he got it from.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious: if the court gave land by שומא to a creditor, and he went and had it given by שומא to his own creditor, we tell that second creditor: you are no better than the man you got it from.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts working out how far the rule of returning שומא land reaches. It says something it calls obvious: a creditor's creditor also has to give the land back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first creditor held the land under the condition that the debtor could pay and take it back. When he passes it to his own creditor as payment, the second creditor gets only the rights the first one had. So the original debtor can pay and reclaim the land from him too.

keyTerms.meaning: Court appraisal, where land is valued and given to a creditor as payment
You are no better (your rights are not stronger)

phrases.english: It is obvious: if they appraised land for a creditor,
and he went and had it appraised
for his own creditor,
phrases.notes: This is someone the first creditor owed money to, so he paid him with this same land.

phrases.english: we say to him:
you are no better
than the man you came from.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the הלכה of אמימר (returning שומא land) to a case where the land passed on to a second creditor.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A creditor's creditor who received שומא land must return it when the original debtor pays.

steps.title: Buyers, heirs and gift receivers keep the land
steps.stepSummary: If the creditor sold the שומא land, left it to heirs, or gave it as a gift, the debtor cannot take it back from them. They came in to own the land itself, not to collect money.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he sold it, left it as an inheritance, or gave it as a gift, then certainly these people came in from the start to get the land, not to get money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets the other side of the line. When the land reached someone through a sale, inheritance or gift, it is not returned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A creditor's creditor took the land in place of money, so paying him money makes sense. A buyer, heir or gift receiver never had a debt to collect. They came to own the land itself, so the debtor's offer of money does not undo their ownership.

keyTerms.meaning: He left it as an inheritance
He came in with the intention of getting the land

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix this up with step 30. The creditor's creditor must give the land back, but a buyer, heir or gift receiver does not. The difference is whether the person came for money or for the land itself.

phrases.english: If he sold it, left it as an inheritance, or gave it as a gift,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the creditor who received the land by שומא.

phrases.english: certainly these people, from the start,
came in with the intention of getting the land
and did not come in with the intention of getting money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with step 30. A creditor's creditor must return the land, but people who acquired it as land do not.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שומא land that was sold, inherited or given as a gift is not returned to the debtor, because those owners came in to own the land itself.

steps.title: A husband counts as a buyer of his wife's land
steps.stepSummary: If שומא land was given to a woman who then married, or taken from a woman who then married and died, the husband counts as a לוקח. He does not give the land back, and it is not given back to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: If land was given by שומא to a woman and she married, or land was taken by שומא from a woman and she married and died: a husband counts as a buyer of his wife's property. So he does not give the land back, and we do not give it back to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings two cases involving a married woman. It rules that the husband is treated like a buyer, so the return rule does not apply to him in either direction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first case, the wife was the creditor. Since the husband is like a buyer, he is like the people in step 31 and does not have to give the land back. In the second case, the wife was the debtor and died. The husband takes her place only as a buyer, not as her heir, so he cannot pay her debt and demand the land back.

keyTerms.meaning: A husband counts as a buyer of his wife's property

phrases.english: If they appraised land for a woman and she married,
or they appraised land from a woman,
and she married and died,
a husband counts as a buyer of his wife's property,
so he does not give the land back
and we do not give it back to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the idea from step 31 that buyers are not part of the return rule, and applies it to a husband.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Since a husband is a לוקח of his wife's property, he neither returns שומא land nor gets שומא land returned to him.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the return rule depends on how a person holds the land: as a creditor or heir, or as a buyer.

steps.title: The source: the תקנת אושא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports the rule that a husband is a לוקח with רבי יוסי בר חנינא's report of the תקנה made in אושא. If a wife sells her נכסי מלוג during the marriage and dies, the husband takes the land back from the buyers.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי יוסי בר חנינא said: in אושא they made a rule that if a woman sold some of her נכסי מלוג while her husband was alive, and then she died, the husband takes the land back from the buyers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source for its claim that a husband counts as a buyer of his wife's property: the תקנה from אושא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the husband were only his wife's heir, he would be stuck with her sale, because an heir cannot undo what the person he inherits from did. The תקנה lets him take the land from the buyers, which shows his rights are like those of a buyer from the time of the marriage, earlier than theirs. That is why step 32 calls him a לוקח.

keyTerms.meaning: The town where the חכמים made several תקנות
Wife's property that stays hers, while the husband gets the produce

steps.whatToRemember: The return of שומא land applies to the debtor's creditor and to a creditor's creditor, who came for money. It does not apply to buyers, heirs, gift receivers, or a husband, who is a לוקח according to the תקנת אושא.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina said:
In Usha they enacted:
a woman who sold some of her melog property
while her husband was alive, and then she died,
the husband takes it back from the buyers.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא: בְּאוּשָׁא הִתְקִינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for step 32's statement that a husband counts as a לוקח.
steps.raayaObject: The principle בעל בנכסי אשתו לוקח הוי
steps.raayaSupportSource: The תקנת אושא reported by רבי יוסי בר חנינא: a husband takes back from buyers the נכסי מלוג his wife sold during the marriage.
